hipaa-foundations: HIPAA exists so people can trust that their health information is used for their care, and for nothing else.
The Privacy Rule: who may use or share information, and why.
The Security Rule: how electronic information is kept safe.
The Breach Notification Rule: what happens when it is exposed.
ERS is bound by an agreement.
Anyone ERS uses makes the same promise.
And you are the last link.
Education: everyone knows the rules and why.
Commitment: everyone does their part, even when nobody is watching.
Culture: asking and reporting feel normal.
Open a record only to complete the task you were given.
Looking up a neighbor or friend is not allowed, even if the system lets you in.
Nor is copying records to your phone.
hipaa-phi: PHI is health information that identifies a person, in any form.
It is about their health, their care, or payment for it.
There are eighteen identifiers, and a name is only one of them.
HIPAA has two ways to de-identify information, Safe Harbor and Expert Determination. Taking the name out is not one.
A file name with a patient's name.
An email subject line or calendar invite.
A sticky note or printed schedule.
Taking the name out and sending it on as safe is not de-identifying.
De-identifying is the client's decision and process, so ask your lead.
hipaa-privacy: The Privacy Rule works like a locked door. Information may be used and shared only in the ways the rule lists.
Almost everything else needs the patient's written authorization, including marketing and sale.
Treatment, payment and healthcare operations are allowed without a form.
Sharing with the patient, and with HHS when it investigates, is always allowed.
Minimum necessary: send the invoice number and amount.
Too much is sending the full chart to answer a billing question.
Before you send anything, ask five questions. If any answer is not sure, do not send.
Who? Is the recipient the right, authorized person?
What? Is it only the minimum needed?
Why? Is there a task-related reason?
Where? Is it the approved system or address?
How? Is the method approved and secure?
hipaa-rights: The information in a patient's record is about them, so the Privacy Rule gives patients rights over it.
Access: see and copy their records.
Accounting: a list of certain disclosures.
Confidential communications: a different method or place.
Complaint: to the clinic or to HHS.
The clinic generally answers an access request within 30 days.
It acts on a correction request within 60 days.
An accounting covers the six years before the request.
Do not send or change records yourself.
Pass it on the client's way, the same day.
hipaa-associates: A business associate does work for a covered entity that involves patient information. ERS is one for many of its clients.
The clinic shares information only after a signed agreement.
ERS needs an agreement with each vendor it uses.
The same restrictions follow down the chain.
Use information only as the contract allows.
Report any use the contract does not allow, including breaches.
Make subcontractors agree to the same restrictions.
A business associate reports a breach without unreasonable delay, and within 60 days at most.
So report a possible incident internally the same day.
hipaa-security: The Security Rule protects electronic patient information, so that the allowed uses are the only uses that happen.
Confidentiality: only the right people can see it.
Integrity: it has not been changed by mistake or on purpose.
Availability: people can get to it when they need it.
Technical: unique logins, encryption and automatic log-off.
Physical: protecting rooms, workstations and devices.
Administrative: policies, training and risk analysis.
Rate how likely and how harmful.
Act, and document what was decided.
Lock your computer when you step away.
Report a lost or stolen device immediately.
hipaa-incidents: An incident is anything that may have exposed patient information, or broken a rule. If you wonder whether it is an incident, report it.
An incident is reported by anyone, the same day.
A breach is decided by the client and ERS after an assessment, not by you.
The clock starts the day anyone in the workforce knows.
ERS tells the client right away.
Within 60 days, the client tells each affected person, in writing.
Stop what you are doing with the information.
Tell your lead and HR immediately.
Describe what happened, without patient names.
Do not delete or edit records.
hipaa-enforcement: OCR investigates complaints and breach reports. Most cases end before a penalty, and good faith helps.
A complaint or breach report reaches OCR.
It asks for policies, risk analyses and records.
Guidance, an agreement with a plan, or a penalty.
Civil penalties rise with what the organization knew.
Willful neglect, not fixed, is the top tier.
Then willful neglect, fixed within 30 days.
And not knowing at the bottom.
Knowingly disclosing health information: up to 1 year.
Under false pretenses: up to 5 years.
For gain or malicious harm: up to 10 years.
Opening records with no work reason.
A stolen laptop and no risk analysis to show.
A patient story posted without a signed authorization.
hipaa-state_laws: HIPAA is the floor, not the ceiling. A state law that protects patients more still applies, and the stricter rule wins.
Texas requires new hires to be trained within 90 days.
A Texas provider with an electronic record answers a written request within 15 business days.
Signed training statements are kept for six years.
California licensed clinics and hospitals report breaches within 15 business days.
California businesses in general tell affected residents within 30 calendar days. A licensed clinic can fall under both rules.
Check which state the client is in.
hipaa-lab_public: On the phone, never confirm that someone is a patient. Offer to take a message.
Can you tell me if my neighbor is a patient at your clinic?
I can't confirm or share anything about anyone. I can take a message, in case she is a patient.
You neither confirm nor deny, and the message lets her decide.
A reply with visit details confirms the person was a patient.
A safe reply invites them to contact the office, and the client approves it.
Is any patient in it: a name, photo, story or date?
Is there a signed authorization for this exact use?
Does it confirm someone is a patient, even without a name?
hipaa-lab_records: Payment work is allowed, but only for the minimum information each step needs.
Export only the columns the review needs.
Share only what the eligibility check needs.
Do not export every field to save time.
Do not send the whole chart to answer a billing question.
The clinic holds the patient information.
A collection agency is a business associate, so it needs a signed agreement.
Only then may it receive anything.
Content: only what the step needs.
